nemet-juhaszkutya.tagline: Clever, loyal and always ready for a job.
nemet-juhaszkutya.leiras: The German Shepherd was founded by Max von Stephanitz in 1899 as a versatile herding and working dog. Clever, loyal and highly trainable, it holds its own almost everywhere, from police work and search and rescue to guide dog work. It bonds closely with its family and is reserved with strangers, so it needs early socialisation and consistent training. Be prepared for heavy shedding all year round, and for a dog that soon gets bored without a job.
nemet-juhaszkutya.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, both physical exercise and mental tasks
nemet-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: The four-legged star of the popular Austrian crime series “Inspector Rex” (Kommissar Rex) was a German Shepherd too.
malinois.tagline: Elite athlete in a fur coat – only for experienced, active owners.
malinois.leiras: The Malinois is one of the four varieties of the Belgian Shepherd, named after the city of Mechelen (Malines in French). An extremely fast, tireless and work-obsessed breed, it is now one of the most sought-after dogs of police forces and armies worldwide. A well-occupied Malinois is a devoted, cooperative companion, but a daily walk is not enough for it: it needs regular, serious work. Bored, it can quickly become tense and destructive, so it suits mainly experienced owners who do dog sports.
malinois.mozgas: 2+ hours a day of intense exercise and regular work
malinois.erdekesseg: The US Secret Service also employs Malinois to guard the White House.
border-collie.tagline: The genius of the dog world: if you don’t give it a job, it will find one.
border-collie.leiras: The Border Collie developed as the working dog of shepherds in the English–Scottish border country and is still one of the world’s best herders. Extremely clever, attentive and hungry for work, it learns lightning fast and is almost unbeatable in dog sports (agility, obedience, herding). If it doesn’t get enough mental and physical work, it finds some for itself – for instance, by trying to herd cars, cyclists or children. It is happy in a family too, but only if the lifestyle is truly active.
border-collie.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with plenty of mental challenges
tervueren.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with plenty of mental challenges
border-collie.erdekesseg: An American Border Collie called Chaser learned to recognise more than a thousand of its toys by name, and the dog’s abilities were even documented in a scientific paper.
ausztral-juhaszkutya.tagline: Colourful-coated bundle of energy that herds the family too.
ausztral-juhaszkutya.leiras: Despite its name, the Australian Shepherd developed on farms in the western United States and became truly well known at rodeos in the mid-20th century. A clever, enthusiastic and highly trainable herder, it bonds closely with its family and can be wary of strangers at first. With an active owner it makes a great sports and hiking partner, but without a job it soon gets bored and may start herding children or other animals. Its thick coat sheds heavily, so brushing several times a week is essential.
ausztral-juhaszkutya.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with running and tasks
dobermann.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with running and tasks
ausztral-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: Australian Shepherds often have two different-coloured eyes – or two colours within a single eye – which is completely accepted in the breed.
shetlandi-juhaszkutya.tagline: Mini Collie with a big heart – and an even bigger voice.
shetlandi-juhaszkutya.leiras: The Sheltie developed on Scotland’s Shetland Islands as a small herding dog and was later crossed with the Rough Collie as well. Gentle, sensitive and highly trainable, it is very attached to its owner and rather reserved with strangers. It can live happily in a flat if it gets its daily exercise and shared playtime. Be prepared for a dog that loves to bark, and whose thick coat needs regular brushing and sheds heavily.
shetlandi-juhaszkutya.mozgas: 1 hour of walking a day, with play and learning
shetlandi-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: The breed was originally meant to be recognised as the “Shetland Collie”, but after protests from Collie breeders it ended up with the name Shetland Sheepdog.
welsh-corgi-pembroke.tagline: Short legs, big personality – a royal favourite.
welsh-corgi-pembroke.leiras: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi developed in Pembrokeshire, in south-west Wales, for herding cattle: its low build let it dodge kicks easily. A cheerful, brave and clever dog with a big personality, it loves being the centre of attention. It learns easily and is a good choice for first-time owners, but it may instinctively nip at the heels of running children and likes to bark. It is prone to obesity, which also strains its long back, so watch the portions.
welsh-corgi-pembroke.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking, play and learning
welsh-corgi-pembroke.erdekesseg: During her reign, the British Queen Elizabeth II kept more than thirty corgis, which is why many people still know the breed as the “royal dog” today.
puli.tagline: Walking cloud of dreadlocks: cheerful, nimble and an eternal teenager.
puli.leiras: For centuries the Puli has been the herding dog of Hungarian shepherds, working beside the flocks alongside the larger guard dogs. Nimble, lively and extremely alert, it is devoted to its family, suspicious of strangers and quick to raise the alarm loudly. Its corded coat sheds little but needs careful care: the cords have to be separated by hand, and after a bath the coat can take up to a whole day to dry. Clever but independent-minded, it needs patient, consistent training.
puli.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day, with plenty of play and tasks
puli.erdekesseg: Beast, the dog of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, is a Puli too.
pumi.tagline: Curly, high-spirited Hungarian herder who notices everything.
pumi.leiras: The Pumi developed in Hungary in the 17th–18th centuries, when the ancient Puli was crossed with western, prick-eared, terrier-type herding dogs. Lively, brave and extremely alert, it notices everything and reports on it all loudly. It learns lightning fast, excels in dog sports, is very attached to its family and is reserved with strangers. Its curly coat sheds little and is easy to manage, but without daily exercise and mental tasks, the high-energy, noisy Pumi can quickly become too much to handle.
pumi.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with plenty of running and tasks
pumi.erdekesseg: The American Kennel Club (AKC) officially recognised the Pumi in 2016, and since then it has become better and better known across the Atlantic.
mudi.tagline: Hungary’s secret weapon: versatile, quick to learn, an agility champion.
mudi.leiras: The Mudi arose spontaneously among Hungarian herding dogs in the 18th–19th centuries. Extremely versatile, it herds, guards and also excels in dog sports (agility, flyball, obedience). Clever, brave and quick to learn, it is very attached to its family and gets on well with children, but is alert and noisy towards strangers. Its coat is easy to care for, but the Mudi is a lively working dog that needs daily exercise and mental tasks.
mudi.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, exercise and mental work
mudi.erdekesseg: It was first described as a breed in its own right only in 1936, by Dr Dezső Fényes; until then it had not been sharply distinguished from the Puli and the Pumi.
komondor.tagline: White corded guardian angel that defends its flock at all costs.
komondor.leiras: For centuries the Komondor has been the livestock guardian of Hungarian shepherds: it did not herd, but protected the animals from wolves and thieves. Calm, dignified and independent, it takes guarding the family and territory entrusted to it very seriously and is suspicious of strangers. Its white, corded coat is unique but demands a great deal of care: the cords must be separated regularly, and after a bath the coat can take a day or two to dry. It needs an experienced owner, a spacious fenced yard and early, thorough socialisation.
komondor.mozgas: 1 hour of calm walking a day, plus a patrol of the yard
komondor.erdekesseg: With its white, corded coat it almost blends into a flock of sheep, and the thick cords also protect it from predators’ bites.
kuvasz.tagline: Noble white guardian: gentle with the family, bold with strangers.
kuvasz.leiras: The Kuvasz is an ancient Hungarian livestock guardian that for centuries protected shepherds’ animals from predators. It is gently attached to its family and can be patient with children, but is reserved with strangers and boldly stands up for “its flock”. Bred to make independent decisions, it is not known for blind obedience: it needs patient, consistent training and early socialisation. Its white, wavy coat sheds heavily, and an adult Kuvasz needs plenty of space.
kuvasz.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking a day, plus free roaming in the yard
kuvasz.erdekesseg: After the Second World War the breed was on the brink of extinction and had to be rebuilt from a few surviving dogs.
rottweiler.tagline: Calm strength and devotion – needs consistent training.
rottweiler.leiras: The Rottweiler is named after the German town of Rottweil, where butchers used it to drive cattle and pull carts. Calm, self-assured and extremely loyal, it protects its family naturally and rarely barks without reason. It is highly trainable and happy to work, but because of its great strength it needs consistent, positive training and thorough socialisation from puppyhood. In some countries keeping one requires a permit, so check the local rules.
rottweiler.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking and shared tasks
rottweiler.erdekesseg: In the early 20th century it was officially recognised as a police dog breed in Germany.
dobermann.tagline: Elegant bodyguard, secretly convinced it’s a lapdog.
dobermann.leiras: The breed was developed by Louis Dobermann, a tax collector from Thuringia, in the late 19th century to be a reliable companion and protector. Elegant, energetic and extremely intelligent, it learns quickly and willingly. It is very attached to its family, seeks closeness and is alert with strangers. Its short coat is easy to groom, but it feels the cold and needs plenty of exercise, and because heart muscle disease (cardiomyopathy) is common in the breed, regular heart screening is recommended.
dobermann.erdekesseg: In the Second World War it was one of the main combat dogs of the US Marine Corps; the statue on the war dog memorial in Guam also portrays a Dobermann.
nemet-boxer.tagline: Eternal clown in a muscular body – a children’s favourite.
nemet-boxer.leiras: The Boxer developed in Munich in the late 19th century as a descendant of the old Bullenbeisser (“bull biter”) type of dog. Playful, cheerful and extremely patient with children, it is also an alert watchdog. It matures slowly: it often behaves like a puppy until the age of three, so enthusiastic jumping and pulling on the lead are worth tackling early. Because of its short muzzle it tolerates heat poorly, and in summer exercise must be scheduled for the cooler hours.
nemet-boxer.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day, with lots of play; in summer during the cool hours
nemet-boxer.erdekesseg: In the First World War, Boxers were used as messenger dogs, pack dogs and guard dogs.
torpe-schnauzer.tagline: Bearded little sage and alert watchdog, in pocket size.
torpe-schnauzer.leiras: The Miniature Schnauzer developed in Germany in the late 19th century by crossing the Standard Schnauzer with smaller breeds, originally as a ratter on farms and in stables. A lively, clever and cheerful dog, it is attached to its family and is a good choice for first-time owners. It does very well in a flat, but as an alert watchdog it announces every noise loudly, so it is worth working on barking early. Its wire coat sheds little but needs regular trimming and beard care.
torpe-schnauzer.mozgas: 1 hour of walking a day, with play and nose work
torpe-schnauzer.erdekesseg: The name Schnauzer comes from the German word “Schnauze” (muzzle, snout), referring to the breed’s characteristic bearded muzzle.
cane-corso.tagline: Italian bodyguard: imposing, loyal – a serious responsibility.
cane-corso.leiras: A descendant of the ancient Roman molossers, it guarded estates and livestock in southern Italy for centuries and even helped with big-game hunting. Calm, self-assured and extremely loyal to its family, it is reserved with strangers and takes its guarding role seriously. It is clever and learns willingly, but needs early, thorough socialisation and a consistent, calm hand, so it suits an experienced owner better. In some countries keeping one requires a permit, so check the local rules.
cane-corso.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking, play and shared tasks
bullterrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking, play and shared tasks
cane-corso.erdekesseg: By the mid-20th century it had almost completely disappeared, and it survives only thanks to an Italian rescue programme launched in the 1970s.
nemet-dog.tagline: The Apollo of dogs: giant size, gentle heart.
nemet-dog.leiras: Although its name suggests Danish origins, the Great Dane developed in Germany, originally for wild boar hunting and guarding grand estates. Despite its enormous size it is calm, gentle and very affectionate, happily leans on its owner and is patient with children. At home it is a surprisingly quiet couch potato, but its space needs, appetite and running costs are all enormous too. Sadly it is a short-lived breed, so it is especially important to choose a puppy from health-screened parents.
nemet-dog.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of calm walking a day, with gentle exercise during puppyhood
nemet-dog.erdekesseg: According to Guinness World Records, the tallest dog of all time, Zeus, who stood 111.8 cm at the withers, was a Great Dane – and so is the cartoon hero Scooby-Doo.
berni-pasztorkutya.tagline: Tricolour mountain teddy bear with endless patience.
berni-pasztorkutya.leiras: It was the all-rounder of farms in the Swiss Alps: it pulled small carts, herded livestock and guarded the yard. Calm, good-natured and endlessly patient, especially sweet with children, it doesn’t like to be away from its family for long. It learns willingly and first-time owners can cope with it, but its thick, tricolour coat sheds heavily and it struggles in a heatwave. Sadly it is a short-lived breed, and cancers are more common in it than average.
berni-pasztorkutya.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking a day, in summer during the cool hours
berni-pasztorkutya.erdekesseg: In Switzerland it used to be harnessed to small carts loaded with milk churns, and cart pulling is still a popular dog sport among the breed’s fans.
bernathegyi.tagline: Legendary rescue dog: calm, kindly – and a drooler.
bernathegyi.leiras: It was kept by the monks of the hospice at the Great St Bernard Pass in Switzerland and for generations helped find travellers lost in snowstorms. A calm, kindly and patient giant that practically takes children into its care. It is content with little exercise, but because of its weight, good lead manners and basic obedience matter from puppyhood. Be prepared for drooling, heavy shedding and the fact that it tolerates heat very badly.
bernathegyi.mozgas: About 1 hour of calm walking a day, less in a heatwave
bernathegyi.erdekesseg: Its most famous representative, Barry, is said by tradition to have saved more than 40 people in the early 19th century; his stuffed body can be seen today in the Natural History Museum of Bern.
uj-fundlandi.tagline: Swimming nanny: the gentle giant of water rescue.
uj-fundlandi.leiras: In Canada, on the island of Newfoundland, it was the fishermen’s workmate: it hauled nets, carried loads and rescued people who had fallen into the water. Extremely gentle, patient and well balanced, it is legendarily tender with children and rarely heard barking. Thanks to its webbed feet and water-repellent coat it loves swimming, so the lakeside is its favourite territory. Its thick double coat needs brushing several times a week and sheds heavily, and you must reckon with drooling too.
uj-fundlandi.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, best with some swimming
uj-fundlandi.erdekesseg: A Newfoundland called Seaman accompanied Lewis and Clark’s famous expedition (1804–1806) all the way across North America to the Pacific Ocean.
angol-bulldog.tagline: Grumpy face, heart of gold – a true couch captain.
angol-bulldog.leiras: Its ancestors were used for bull-baiting in England for centuries, but today’s English Bulldog is a far cry from that: a calm, sweet and affectionate companion. It tolerates children well and feels best near the sofa. It can be stubborn, so it is best raised with patience and treats. Because of its flat nose, breathing difficulties are common, and it copes badly with heat and exertion, so only choose one from health-screened parents.
angol-bulldog.mozgas: 2–3 short, calm walks a day, taking it easy in warm weather
napolyi-masztiff.mozgas: 2–3 short, calm walks a day, taking it easy in warm weather
angol-bulldog.erdekesseg: In the Second World War it became a symbol of British resilience, and Winston Churchill was often compared to a Bulldog.
yorkshire-terrier.tagline: Silk-maned little boss, blissfully unaware of its size.
yorkshire-terrier.leiras: In 19th-century northern England, in the factories and mines of Yorkshire and Lancashire, it was a ratter, and only later became the darling of the drawing rooms. Its tiny body holds a big terrier soul: brave, lively, curious, very attached to its owner, and happy to bark at anything that moves. It sheds little, but its long, silky coat needs daily combing or regular clipping short. It is fragile, so it needs supervision around small children, and its teeth need regular care too.
yorkshire-terrier.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking and play a day
bichon-frise.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking and play a day
lhasa-apso.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking and play a day
coton-de-tulear.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking and play a day
yorkshire-terrier.erdekesseg: In the Second World War, a Yorkshire Terrier named Smoky crawled through a narrow pipe in the Philippines, pulling a telegraph wire through it, so the soldiers did not have to start days of risky digging.
jack-russell-terrier.tagline: Spring-legged little hunter with inexhaustible energy.
jack-russell-terrier.leiras: It is named after the English clergyman John “Jack” Russell, who in the early 19th century bred these nimble little terriers for fox hunting. Cheerful, pushy and astonishingly tenacious: if it isn’t given a job, it quickly finds one, such as digging up the garden or chewing furniture. Clever but strong-willed, it needs consistent, playful training, and in dog sports it is a real little champion. Because of its strong hunting instinct, take care around cats and small pets, and when letting it off the lead.
jack-russell-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of active exercise a day, with plenty of play and tasks
jack-russell-terrier.erdekesseg: Uggie, the canine star of the Oscar-winning film “The Artist”, was a Jack Russell Terrier too.
west-highland-white-terrier.tagline: Snow-white, self-assured little Scot with plenty of humour.
west-highland-white-terrier.leiras: It was bred in the Scottish Highlands from small terriers working on rocky ground to hunt foxes and rodents. A confident, cheerful and friendly little dog with plenty of terrier independence and humour, it loves being at the centre of the family. It copes well in a flat and first-time owners get along with it, but it likes to bark, and outdoors it craves adventure. It has sensitive skin: allergic dermatitis is common, and its wiry coat needs regular trimming.
west-highland-white-terrier.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking and play a day
west-highland-white-terrier.erdekesseg: It used to be called the Poltalloch Terrier too, after the Scottish Malcolm family’s estate, where the white line was deliberately bred.
staffordshire-bullterrier.tagline: Muscle giant in a small package that adores its people.
staffordshire-bullterrier.leiras: It developed in 19th-century England, in the county of Staffordshire, and quickly became a favourite companion of working-class families. Muscular, strong and brave, yet extremely people-loving and famously patient with children. Energetic, so it needs lots of play and exercise, but it doesn’t always get on with other dogs, so early socialisation is important. In some countries keeping one requires a permit or is restricted, so check the local rules.
staffordshire-bullterrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking, running and shared play
staffordshire-bullterrier.erdekesseg: The British Kennel Club’s breed standard specifically highlights that the Staffie is especially devoted to children.
amerikai-staffordshire-terrier.tagline: Strong, brave and devoted – best in experienced hands.
amerikai-staffordshire-terrier.leiras: It developed in the United States in the 19th century from English bulldog–terrier type dogs brought over from England, and grew larger and stronger than its English cousin. Strong, brave and very affectionate, it is sweet with its family and often a real clown who loves to be near its owner. It needs an experienced, consistent owner and early socialisation, because it does not always get along with other dogs. In some countries keeping one requires a licence or is restricted, so find out about the local rules in advance.
amerikai-staffordshire-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walking, running and strength-based play
amerikai-staffordshire-terrier.erdekesse: In 1936 the American Kennel Club still recognised it as the “Staffordshire Terrier”; it received its present name in 1972, to tell it apart from its smaller English relative.
tacsko.tagline: Long body, huge courage – the badger hunter who rules the sofa too.
tacsko.leiras: Bred in Germany for badger and fox hunting: its name (Dachshund) literally means “badger dog” in German, and its short legs helped it in the burrow. Brave, curious and very affectionate, but also strong-willed, and it announces everything with loud barking. It comes in three coat varieties (short, long and wire-haired) and several sizes, so it can fit into many kinds of homes. Because of its long spine it is prone to intervertebral disc disease, so avoid lots of stair climbing, jumping and excess weight.
tacsko.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day with plenty of sniffing, no jumping
tacsko.erdekesseg: The mascot of the 1972 Munich Olympics, the stripy Waldi, was a Dachshund – the first official Olympic mascot.
sziberiai-husky.tagline: Ice-blue-eyed escape artist who would rather sing than bark.
sziberiai-husky.leiras: In north-eastern Siberia the Chukchi people bred it for sled pulling; it reached Alaska in the early 20th century and spread from there worldwide. A friendly, cheerful pack dog that gets along with almost everyone, so it is not at all suited as a guard dog. It rarely barks, but is all the keener to howl and “sing”, and with its huge need for exercise it is a true escape artist, so it needs a tall, secure fence. Independent-minded, it finds recall hard to learn, and twice a year it sheds its undercoat in huge amounts.
sziberiai-husky.mozgas: 2 hours a day or more, ideally with running and pulling
sziberiai-husky.erdekesseg: In 1925 sled dogs carried diphtheria serum in a relay to Nome, Alaska, which was struck by an epidemic; the two most famous lead dogs, Balto and Togo, were Siberian Huskies too.
szamojed.tagline: A smiling snow cloud who counts everyone as a friend.
szamojed.leiras: It is named after the Siberian Samoyedic peoples (including the Nenets), who kept it for reindeer herding, sled pulling and companionship. An extremely friendly, cheerful and sociable dog: it regards everyone as a friend, so it is no guard dog, but it adores children. A chatty dog that likes to bark and “comment”, and when bored or left alone a lot, it lets you know loudly. Its snow-white, thick coat sheds heavily and needs regular, thorough brushing, and it finds great summer heat hard to bear.
szamojed.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day of walking, running and play – in summer, during the cool hours
szamojed.erdekesseg: Genetic studies place the Samoyed among the most ancient dog breeds, alongside the likes of the Siberian Husky or the Akita.
pomeraniai-torpespicc.tagline: A fluffy pompom with a surprisingly big voice.
pomeraniai-torpespicc.leiras: A descendant of the larger German Spitzes, it is named after Pomerania on the Baltic Sea, and it acquired its tiny size largely in 19th-century England, as Queen Victoria’s favourite. A lively, curious and confident little dog that loves attention and barks at every little noise. Ideal in a flat and a loyal companion, but it is fragile, so it is less recommended around small children. Its thick double coat needs regular brushing and sheds heavily.
pomeraniai-torpespicc.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking a day plus play indoors
pomeraniai-torpespicc.erdekesseg: Only three dogs survived the 1912 Titanic disaster, and two of them were Pomeranians.
shiba-inu.tagline: Cat-hearted Japanese rebel: clean, independent, stubborn.
shiba-inu.leiras: The Shiba Inu hunted small game in the mountains of Japan and is the smallest of the six native Japanese breeds. A clean, almost cat-like self-groomer and an independent dog that is attached to its family, but prefers to be petted in its own time. It barks little, but if something displeases it, it protests with a loud “Shiba scream”. Because of its strong hunting instinct and stubbornness its recall is unreliable, so on walks it mostly stays on the lead.
shiba-inu.mozgas: 1 hour of walking a day, mostly on the lead
shiba-inu.erdekesseg: The star of the world-famous “Doge” internet meme, the Japanese dog called Kabosu, was also a Shiba Inu.
akita-inu.leiras: The Akita comes from the mountains of Japan’s northern Akita Prefecture, where it was once used to hunt big game and also kept as a guard dog. A dignified, calm and quiet dog that is deeply loyal to its family but reserved with strangers. It is well balanced at home, but strong-willed, and often does not get on with other dogs – especially of the same sex. It needs early, thorough socialisation and a confident, consistent owner, so it is not recommended for beginners.
akita-inu.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of calm, regular walks
akita-inu.erdekesseg: The most famous Akita, Hachiko, waited every day for nearly ten years for his late owner at Shibuya station in Tokyo, where a statue now keeps his memory alive.
beagle.tagline: A cheerful pack dog who thinks with his nose – always ready to make a break for it.
beagle.leiras: The Beagle developed in England, where it followed the scent of hares in a pack. Cheerful, friendly and patient, it gets on well with children and other dogs, and finds its pack in its family. But its nose always leads the way: when it catches an interesting scent, it forgets the recall, and it is a clever escape artist. It signals with loud, drawn-out baying, and when left alone it gets bored, so not every neighbour will love it.
beagle.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking a day, with plenty of sniffing
beagle.erdekesseg: Snoopy, the world-famous character of the Peanuts comics, is a Beagle too – and thanks to their excellent noses, in several countries they are used at airports to sniff out banned food in luggage.
dalmata.tagline: Spotted running champion who needs loads of exercise.
dalmata.leiras: The Dalmatian is named after Dalmatia in Croatia and became famous in the 18th–19th centuries as an escort and guard dog running alongside horse-drawn carriages. That is the source of its enormous stamina, which has lasted to this day: an energetic, playful, people-oriented dog and an excellent running partner. Despite its short coat it sheds heavily all year round, and the needle-like hairs get stuck in everything. Without exercise and activity it gets bored and destructive, and its boisterous play can be too much for small children.
dalmata.mozgas: 2 hours a day, including running or cycling
dalmata.erdekesseg: Dalmatian puppies are born pure white; their characteristic spots only begin to appear in the first weeks.
erdelyi-kopo.tagline: Hunter of the Carpathians: tenacious, brave, with a ringing voice.
erdelyi-kopo.leiras: For centuries the Transylvanian Hound has been the hunting dog of the Carpathian forests, signalling the trail of game with its ringing, far-carrying voice. Well balanced, good-natured, brave and extremely tenacious, it is faithfully devoted to its family and gets on well with children too. When hunting it works independently, so once it picks up a scent it is hard to call back. It needs a spacious, well-fenced garden and plenty of exercise, and does not feel at home in a flat or in city life.
erdelyi-kopo.mozgas: 2 hours a day or more, with lots of exercise out in open country
erdelyi-kopo.erdekesseg: There used to be two varieties: the long-legged one was used for big game, the short-legged one for fox and hare – today you almost only meet the long-legged type.
basset-hound.tagline: Floppy ears, soulful eyes, endless calm (and a nose).
basset-hound.leiras: The Basset Hound developed in France, where hunters on foot used these low-slung dogs with excellent scenting ability to follow the trail of hares. Calm, gentle and patient, friendly with children and other dogs, and a true sofa-dweller at home. On walks, however, its nose is in charge: it stubbornly follows scents, and likes to bay in its deep, booming voice. Its long back and drooping ears need careful attention, and expect drooling too.
basset-hound.mozgas: 1 hour of leisurely walking a day, with plenty of sniffing
basset-hound.erdekesseg: Its name comes from the French “bas” (low), which refers to its short legs.
rhodesiai-ridgeback.tagline: “Ridged” back, calm, strong, an independent thinker.
rhodesiai-ridgeback.leiras: The Rhodesian Ridgeback developed in South Africa from the dogs of European settlers and the local, ridge-backed Khoikhoi dogs; it is named after the strip of hair on its back that grows in the opposite direction. At home it is calm, dignified and loyal, gentle with its family and reserved with strangers. It barks little, but it is a strong, independent thinker, so it needs early socialisation and patient, consistent training. Because of its strong hunting instinct it may chase smaller animals.
rhodesiai-ridgeback.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with free running in a fenced area
rhodesiai-ridgeback.erdekesseg: It was once also called the “African lion dog”, because in a small pack it could hold a lion at bay until the hunter arrived.
magyar-vizsla.tagline: Golden-brown Velcro dog: always at its owner’s side.
magyar-vizsla.leiras: The Hungarian Vizsla has been the companion of hunters in the Carpathian Basin for centuries. A sensitive, extremely affectionate breed that is happiest close to its owner, so it is not suited to a kennel or to long periods alone. It learns quickly, but cannot bear harsh treatment. If it gets its daily proper run and is raised with positive reinforcement, it is an excellent family and sports companion – without exercise, however, it can become restless and destructive.
magyar-vizsla.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with plenty of off-lead running
magyar-vizsla.erdekesseg: Several times in its history – most recently after the Second World War – it came close to extinction, but breeders revived it from a few surviving dogs.
drotszoru-magyar-vizsla.tagline: The bearded, hard-wearing Vizsla – at home in water and thick undergrowth.
drotszoru-magyar-vizsla.leiras: The Hungarian Wirehaired Vizsla came into being in the first half of the 20th century to be a hunting dog that works tirelessly even on harsh, cold and wet terrain. Like its short-haired relative it is affectionate, quick to learn and sensitive, and patient with children, with a somewhat sturdier build. Its harsh, dense coat protects it well; weekly brushing and the occasional hand-stripping are enough. It needs plenty of exercise and tasks, and is unhappy when left alone or idle.
drotszoru-magyar-vizsla.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with free running, even swimming
drotszoru-magyar-vizsla.erdekesseg: It was created in the 1930s by crossing Hungarian Vizslas with German Wirehaired Pointers, so that it would cope better with cold and water.
weimari-vizsla.leiras: The Weimaraner became known in the 19th century as the hunting dog of the grand ducal court of Weimar; you can recognise it from afar by its silver-grey colour and pale eyes. Intelligent, energetic and extremely devoted, it follows its owner like a shadow, and it has guarding instincts too. Left alone it is prone to separation anxiety, and when bored it destroys things or makes a racket. Because of its strong will and hunting instinct it needs an experienced, consistent owner and plenty of exercise every day.
weimari-vizsla.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with running and mental challenges
weimari-vizsla.erdekesseg: Since the 1970s the American art photographer William Wegman has become world-famous for his humorous, often costumed pictures featuring Weimaraners.
rovidszoru-nemet-vizsla.tagline: Hunter and athlete, ready for any terrain.
rovidszoru-nemet-vizsla.leiras: The German Shorthaired Pointer (Kurzhaar) was born in 19th-century Germany as a true all-rounder: it points game, retrieves, follows a trail and works in water too. A cheerful, friendly, quick-to-learn dog, patient with children, with almost inexhaustible stamina. At home it is calm only if it has been thoroughly tired out outdoors beforehand, otherwise it gets bored, destructive or tries to escape. It stays puppy-like and bouncy for a long time, so it needs several hours of active programme every day.
rovidszoru-nemet-vizsla.mozgas: 2 hours a day or more, mostly running
rovidszoru-nemet-vizsla.erdekesseg: In 2016 a German Shorthaired Pointer named CJ won Best in Show at the prestigious Westminster dog show in New York.
ir-szetter.tagline: Red silk, eternal high spirits and lots of running.
ir-szetter.leiras: The Irish Setter developed in 18th–19th-century Ireland for bird hunting: when it finds game, it signals by freezing and crouching low – hence its name (English “to set”). Cheerful and friendly, it likes children and other dogs, and is a true eternal teenager. It matures slowly, stays scatty and easily distracted for a long time, so training takes patience. Its silky red coat must be brushed several times a week, and it needs masses of running.
ir-szetter.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with plenty of off-lead running
ir-szetter.erdekesseg: The solid red setter became dominant in the 19th century; the older red-and-white type is now a separate breed, the Irish Red and White Setter.
labrador-retriever.tagline: Everyone’s best friend – and the rightful owner of every dropped morsel.
labrador-retriever.leiras: The Labrador’s ancestors were helpers to fishermen on the island of Newfoundland; the breed was shaped into a gundog in 19th-century England. Friendly, cooperative and easy to train, so it is one of the world’s most popular family, guide and assistance dogs. It loves eating, swimming and carrying everything in its mouth, but when young it is rather boisterous and chewy. It is prone to obesity, sheds plenty, and without daily exercise and mental tasks it gets bored.
labrador-retriever.mozgas: 1.5 hours a day, with retrieving and swimming
labrador-retriever.erdekesseg: A 2016 study in Cambridge showed that many Labradors carry a faulty variant of the POMC gene, which increases the feeling of hunger – which is why they are so greedy.
golden-retriever.tagline: Sunshine on four paws: patient, kind and in love with carrying things about.
golden-retriever.leiras: The Golden Retriever was born in 19th-century Scotland as a gundog that retrieves gently from both water and thick cover. Patient, kind and friendly with everyone, excellent with children and happy to learn – but not suited as a watchdog. It loves water, mud and playing together. Its long coat sheds heavily and needs brushing several times a week, and cancers are more common in the breed than average.
golden-retriever.mozgas: 1.5 hours a day, with plenty of play and retrieving
golden-retriever.erdekesseg: The first Golden litter was born in 1868 in Scotland on Lord Tweedmouth’s estate, from the mating of a yellow retriever called Nous and a Tweed Water Spaniel called Belle.
angol-cocker-spaniel.tagline: A cheerful, flop-eared hunter who wants to be part of the family.
angol-cocker-spaniel.leiras: The English Cocker Spaniel is the classic British dog for hunting winged game: it flushes birds out of thick undergrowth and brings them back. A cheerful, endlessly tail-wagging, people-oriented breed that wants to take part in every family activity. Thanks to its size it can also be kept in a flat, as long as it is exercised daily. Its silky coat and long ears need regular brushing, trimming and ear cleaning, and the working lines are much more energetic than the show type.
angol-cocker-spaniel.erdekesseg: It takes its name from the woodcock, a game bird it was once an excellent helper in hunting.
angol-springer-spaniel.tagline: Tireless, friendly, a lover of water and mud.
angol-springer-spaniel.leiras: The English Springer Spaniel is the classic flushing and retrieving dog of the British hunting fields. Friendly, cheerful and very affectionate, it gets on brilliantly with children too, and learns quickly and willingly. Its energy is almost inexhaustible: water, mud and thick undergrowth are its true terrain, so its drooping ears and wavy coat need regular grooming. With too little exercise and activity it gets bored and restless, so it is not a sofa dog.
angol-springer-spaniel.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with plenty of free running and swimming
angol-springer-spaniel.erdekesseg: Its name comes from the English verb “to spring”, meaning to flush game: its job was to make game burst out of the bushes in front of the hunter.
lagotto-romagnolo.tagline: Curly truffle hunter that barely sheds.
lagotto-romagnolo.leiras: The Lagotto Romagnolo was originally a water retriever in the marshes of Romagna in northern Italy, and today it is a truffle-hunting specialist. Balanced, friendly and quick to learn, it gets on well with children, and nose work and shared tasks make it happy. Its curly coat sheds little but needs regular brushing and clipping every few months, otherwise it mats. It has a strong urge to sniff and dig, so expect a hole or two in the garden.
lagotto-romagnolo.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours, with plenty of scent games
lagotto-romagnolo.erdekesseg: Its name comes from the Romagna dialect phrase “can lagòt”, meaning water dog, because it originally retrieved waterfowl from the marshes of the Comacchio lagoons.
francia-bulldog.tagline: Bat-eared city star – just keep an eye on its breathing.
francia-bulldog.leiras: The French Bulldog’s ancestors came to France in the 19th century with English lace-makers, and became real stars on the streets of Paris. A cheerful, affectionate and distinctly quiet companion: it barely barks (though it can snore), and gets along fine in a small flat. Its exercise needs are moderate, but it is not lazy – it likes to play and clown around. Because of its flat nose, breathing difficulties are common (brachycephalic syndrome), and it tolerates heat poorly, so choose a puppy only from health-screened parents.
francia-bulldog.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of calm walking a day, in hot weather only when it is cool
francia-bulldog.erdekesseg: In 2022, based on American Kennel Club (AKC) registrations, the French Bulldog became the most popular breed in the USA, knocking the Labrador Retriever off the throne after 31 years.
mopsz.tagline: Wrinkly little comedian who follows you everywhere.
mopsz.leiras: The Pug is an ancient Chinese breed brought to Europe by Dutch traders in the 16th–17th centuries, where it quickly became a favourite of the royal courts. A cheerful, affectionate little comedian who follows you everywhere, patient with children and friendly with strangers too. It is content with little exercise and does well in a flat, but sheds surprisingly heavily. Because of its flat nose, breathing difficulties are common (brachycephalic syndrome), and it tolerates heat poorly, so choose only from health-screened parents.
mopsz.mozgas: 30–45 minutes of easy walking a day, shorter in hot weather
mopsz.erdekesseg: The breed’s old motto is the Latin “multum in parvo”, meaning “much in little”.
chihuahua.tagline: The smallest dog with the biggest self-confidence.
chihuahua.leiras: The Chihuahua comes from Mexico and is the world’s smallest dog breed – though it has no idea. Brave, lively and very affectionate, it often bonds truly with just one person and can be wary of strangers. Thanks to its tiny size you can take it almost anywhere, and it gets plenty of exercise indoors too. It tends to bark a lot, and because of its fragile bones it is less suitable for families with small children.
chihuahua.mozgas: A 20–40-minute walk daily, plus lots of play at home
chihuahua.erdekesseg: It is named after the Mexican state of Chihuahua, and the Guinness World Records title of “smallest living dog” has mostly been held by Chihuahuas.
cavalier-king-charles-spaniel.tagline: Big-eyed and gentle – the king of lapdogs.
cavalier-king-charles-spaniel.leiras: The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel takes its name from King Charles II of England, who adored little spaniels. Gentle, friendly and exceptionally people-oriented, it gets on well with children, older people and other dogs, but is no good at all as a watchdog. A flexible companion that is equally happy on the sofa or on a longer walk. You should know, though, that mitral valve disease (MVD) and syringomyelia are very common in the breed, so choose only from parents that have been heart-screened and MRI-screened.
cavalier-king-charles-spaniel.mozgas: A 45–60-minute walk daily, with some off-lead running
cavalier-king-charles-spaniel.erdekesseg: The modern Cavalier was reborn in the 1920s, when an American, Roswell Eldridge, offered prize money at the Crufts show for breeding back the longer-nosed spaniels known from old paintings.
shih-tzu.tagline: Chrysanthemum-faced little lion – born for a palace.
shih-tzu.leiras: The Shih Tzu comes from Tibet and the Chinese imperial court, where it was pampered as a palace dog for centuries. A friendly, even-tempered and cheerful companion that would rather choose your lap than a long hike, and a good choice for a first-time owner. Its long coat sheds little but needs daily brushing or regular clipping. Because of its short muzzle, breathing difficulties (brachycephalic syndrome) can occur and it copes poorly with heat, so choose from health-screened parents.
shih-tzu.mozgas: 30–45 minutes of gentle walking and play daily
shih-tzu.erdekesseg: Its name means “lion” in Chinese, and because the hair around its face fans out in a circle, it is also nicknamed the “chrysanthemum-faced dog”.
maltai-selyemkutya.leiras: The Maltese is a lapdog of the Mediterranean region with a history stretching back thousands of years. Lively, playful and very affectionate, it is brave despite its tiny size, feels happiest close to its owner, and alertly raises a loud alarm when the doorbell rings. Its snow-white, silky coat sheds little but needs daily brushing and regular eye cleaning. Tiny and fragile, it does not cope well with rough play from small children, and it does not like being left alone for long.
maltai-selyemkutya.mozgas: 30–45 minutes of walking daily and lots of play
maltai-selyemkutya.erdekesseg: One of the oldest European lapdog breeds: similar little white dogs were already kept and depicted by the ancient Greeks and Romans.
bichon-frise.tagline: A cheerful cotton-wool puff that hardly sheds.
bichon-frise.leiras: The Bichon Frisé descends from Mediterranean lapdogs and was a favourite at the French royal court in the Renaissance. Cheerful, gentle and sociable: it gets on well with children, strangers and other animals too, so it is a good choice for a first-time owner. Its curly coat sheds little but needs regular brushing and a groomer every 4–6 weeks, otherwise it mats. It finds being left alone for long hard to bear, and house-training can take more patience.
bichon-frise.erdekesseg: In the 19th century it went from the palaces to the streets and became a star of fairground performers and circuses, because it learns tricks easily.
havanese.tagline: A friendly little companion with a Cuban dancer’s soul.
havanese.leiras: The Havanese (Havana Bichon) is the national dog of Cuba, descended from the bichons that arrived with Spanish sailors. Cheerful, playful and extremely sociable: it loves being the centre of attention, gets on well with children too, and enjoys learning tricks. Its long, silky coat sheds little but must be brushed several times a week, or kept clipped short. It bonds very closely with its person, so it belongs in a home where it is rarely left alone.
havanese.mozgas: 30–60 minutes of walking and playing together daily
havanese.erdekesseg: After the Cuban Revolution the breed all but vanished in its homeland, and it was revived from a few dogs that had reached the United States with their owners.
uszkar.tagline: A curly genius in four sizes – elegant, sporty, doesn’t shed.
uszkar.leiras: The Poodle was originally a water-retrieving gundog and today lives with us in four sizes – toy, miniature, medium and standard. Extremely clever, quick to learn, sensitive and affectionate, it is a real genius at dog sports and at learning tricks. Its curly coat sheds little but needs clipping every 4–8 weeks and regular brushing. Without mental work and enough exercise it gets bored, and the larger sizes need more running than their elegant looks suggest.
uszkar.mozgas: Depending on size, 45 minutes to 2 hours daily, with plenty of brain teasers
uszkar.erdekesseg: Its name comes from the German “pudeln” (to splash about), and the classic pom-pom clip was originally practical: it protected the joints and chest of a dog working in the water from the cold.
boston-terrier.tagline: A little gentleman in a tuxedo, a cheerful city companion.
boston-terrier.leiras: The Boston Terrier was born in Boston in the late 19th century from English Bulldog and terrier ancestors. Cheerful, friendly and playful, it gets on well with children and is relatively easy to train. It barks little, is adaptable, and is content even in a small flat if it gets enough attention. Because of its short muzzle, however, breathing difficulties (brachycephalic syndrome) can occur, it tolerates heat poorly, and its large eyes are vulnerable – choose only from health-screened parents.
boston-terrier.mozgas: A 45–60-minute walk and play daily, less in hot weather
boston-terrier.erdekesseg: Because of its tuxedo-like markings and charming manners, it is nicknamed the “American Gentleman”, and it is the official dog of the state of Massachusetts.
whippet.tagline: A lightning-fast sprinter outdoors, a sofa statue at home.
whippet.leiras: The Whippet is an English sighthound breed that, despite its medium size, is among the fastest dogs. At home it is quiet, gentle, kind with children and thoroughly cuddly: it happily snoozes on the sofa and rarely barks. Outdoors, though, it is a lightning-fast sprinter that needs regular off-lead runs in a safe, fenced area. Its strong hunting instinct means it may chase cats and rabbits, its recall is not always reliable, and its thin coat means it needs a coat of its own in winter.
whippet.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking daily, including safe sprints
whippet.erdekesseg: In the 19th century, the miners of northern England called it the “poor man’s racehorse”, because in their spare time they raced it and hunted rabbits with it.
magyar-agar.tagline: A tireless Hungarian whirlwind – and a great sleeper after a sprint.
magyar-agar.leiras: The Hungarian Greyhound is an ancient Hungarian hunting dog, used for centuries for hare and fox hunting in the Carpathian Basin. At home it is calm, quiet and affectionate, loyal to its family, and reserved and alert with strangers. Outdoors it is a tireless runner that keeps up the pace not only in sprints but over long distances too, so it needs regular gallops in a safe, fenced area. Its short coat needs hardly any grooming, but its strong hunting instinct means it may chase small animals, and its recall is not always reliable.
magyar-agar.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours daily, including safe off-lead running
saluki.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours daily, including safe off-lead running
magyar-agar.erdekesseg: According to tradition, its ancestors arrived in the Carpathian Basin with the conquering Magyars, so it is regarded as one of the oldest Hungarian dog breeds.
olasz-agar.tagline: A porcelain-fine mini sighthound, elegant even in a jumper.
olasz-agar.leiras: The Italian Greyhound is the smallest sighthound breed and became a true fashion dog at the Italian courts of the Renaissance. Gentle, sensitive and very cuddly, it seeks its owner’s closeness and is not a big barker. With its thin coat and little body fat it feels the cold, needs a jumper in winter, and dislikes cold, rainy weather. Because of its fragile leg bones, big jumps can be dangerous, and house-training takes patience.
olasz-agar.mozgas: A 45–60-minute walk, with the occasional safe sprint
olasz-agar.erdekesseg: King Frederick the Great of Prussia loved his Italian Greyhounds so much that, as he had wished, he was finally buried on the terrace of Sanssouci Palace, next to his dogs.
tervueren.tagline: The Belgian Malinois’s long-haired, elegant sibling – same engine.
tervueren.leiras: The Belgian Tervuren developed in Belgium in the late 19th century and is named after the village of Tervuren near Brussels. An extremely attentive, intelligent and hard-working dog that bonds closely with its owner, is initially reserved with strangers and keeps a watchful eye on its surroundings. It learns quickly and excels at dog sports, but it is sensitive and handles harsh treatment badly. Without a daily task and plenty of exercise it easily becomes tense and wound up, and its long coat needs regular brushing and sheds heavily.
tervueren.erdekesseg: The FCI registers the four varieties of the Belgian Shepherd Dog – Malinois, Tervuren, Groenendael and Laekenois – as a single breed: they differ only in the length, texture and colour of their coat.
groenendael.tagline: A black, silky-coated athlete with a sharp mind and even sharper focus.
groenendael.leiras: The Belgian Groenendael is the black, long-haired variety of the Belgian Shepherd Dog, developed in the late 19th century around Brussels. Sharp-witted, extremely attentive and hard-working, it bonds closely with its family, is reserved with strangers and is a reliable watchdog. It learns quickly and excels at agility, obedience and tracking, but it is sensitive, so positive reinforcement suits it better than a heavy hand. Without a job it soon becomes tense and nervy, and its thick black coat sheds heavily.
groenendael.mozgas: 2 hours daily, with running and working together
groenendael.erdekesseg: It is named after the Groenendael château near Brussels, where its owner, Nicolas Rose, began deliberately breeding black, long-haired shepherd dogs in the late 19th century.
collie.tagline: Lassie’s breed: gentle, clever, and shepherd to a whole family.
collie.leiras: The Rough Collie developed from the sheepdogs of the Scottish Highlands, and Queen Victoria’s fondness for it made it truly fashionable in the 19th century. A gentle, sensitive and very affectionate breed, patient with children and easy and willing to learn, so a good choice for a first-time owner. It is rather reserved with strangers, but not hostile. Be prepared for it to bark readily and a lot, and for its thick coat to need regular, thorough brushing – it sheds an enormous amount when moulting.
collie.mozgas: A 1–1.5-hour walk daily, with play and learning
collie.erdekesseg: Screen Lassie is a female dog, yet she was first played by a male collie called Pal, and his descendants carried on the role for generations.
bearded-collie.tagline: A cheerful, bearded clown whose coat is a hobby all of its own.
bearded-collie.leiras: The Bearded Collie herded sheep and cattle on the Scottish upland pastures, and its shaggy coat stood up well to rain and cold. A cheerful, bouncy, friendly dog that adores every member of the family and gets on brilliantly with children. Clever and quick to learn, but with opinions of its own, so patient, playful training suits it, and it likes to make itself heard. Its long, thick coat is a serious commitment: without thorough brushing several times a week it soon mats.
bearded-collie.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours daily, with plenty of off-lead running and play
bearded-collie.erdekesseg: Puppies are typically born with darker colouring; the coat lightens by adolescence and then often takes on a darker shade again in adulthood.
bobtail.tagline: A teddy-bear cloud in a grey-and-white coat, with endless good cheer.
bobtail.leiras: In England the Old English Sheepdog helped farmers drive cattle and sheep to market; today it is above all a lovable family companion. Cheerful, gentle and patient, it gets on especially well with children and is often a real clown. Trainable, but it sometimes goes its own way, so cheerful, consistent training suits it. Its shaggy coat is the biggest commitment: it needs several hours of brushing a week or a regular professional groomer, it sheds heavily, and it handles heat badly.
bobtail.mozgas: A 1–1.5-hour walk and play daily, going easy in a heatwave
bobtail.erdekesseg: The Beatles’ song “Martha My Dear” takes its title from Paul McCartney’s Old English Sheepdog, Martha.
feher-svajci-juhaszkutya.tagline: A snow-white shepherd, the gentler-natured cousin of the German Shepherd.
feher-svajci-juhaszkutya.leiras: The White Swiss Shepherd Dog descends from white German Shepherds and was recognised as a breed in its own right in Switzerland. Gentle, friendly and very quick to learn, it bonds closely with its family, is patient with children and is reserved rather than suspicious with strangers. Sensitive by nature, it responds best to kind, consistent training and also takes part happily in dog sports. Its snow-white, thick coat sheds heavily all year round and, when moulting, covers practically everything.
feher-svajci-juhaszkutya.mozgas: 1.5 hours of exercise daily, with play and learning
feher-svajci-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: Because in the first half of the 20th century white was a disqualifying fault in the German Shepherd in Germany, the white lines survived mainly in the USA and Canada, and from there they found their way back to Europe.
csehszlovak-farkaskutya.tagline: Looks like a wolf and sometimes thinks like one: for professionals only.
csehszlovak-farkaskutya.leiras: It was created in Czechoslovakia in the 1950s by crossing German Shepherds with Carpathian wolves, originally for border patrol duty. It is very attached to its owner and family, handles being left alone badly, is suspicious of strangers and has a strong hunting instinct. Clever but independent-minded: it learns the classic obedience exercises only through patient, consistent work. It rarely barks, preferring to howl, and is a skilled escape artist, so it is recommended only for an experienced owner who can devote plenty of time to it.
csehszlovak-farkaskutya.mozgas: 2+ hours daily, with running, hiking and tasks
csehszlovak-farkaskutya.erdekesseg: The mother of the first wolf–dog litter was a Carpathian she-wolf named Brita, and the father was a German Shepherd named Cézar.
ausztral-pasztorkutya.tagline: A tough, tenacious herder who never asks when we’re going home.
ausztral-pasztorkutya.leiras: The Australian Cattle Dog developed in 19th-century Australia: the drovers’ cattle dogs were crossed with dingoes, among others, so that they could cope with the heat and long journeys. A tough, tenacious and extremely hard-working herder that bonds especially with one or two people and is reserved and alert with strangers. Clever and quick to learn, but independent, so it needs consistent training and a regular job. From herding instinct it tends to nip at heels, which can be unpleasant around small children.
ausztral-pasztorkutya.mozgas: 2 hours of intense exercise daily and a regular job
ausztral-pasztorkutya.erdekesseg: For a long time the Guinness World Records listed an Australian Cattle Dog named Bluey as the oldest dog ever: it lived for more than 29 years.
torpe-pinscher.leiras: The Miniature Pinscher is an old German breed that originally worked as a ratter in stables and farmyards. A lively, brave and curious little dog, a true watchdog that reacts to every little sound with loud barking. Clever, but prone to stubbornness and escaping, so it needs consistent training and a secure fence. Less recommended for families with small children, as it is fragile and does not tolerate rough handling; with its short coat it gets cold easily in winter.
torpe-pinscher.mozgas: A 45–60-minute walk and lively play daily
torpe-pinscher.erdekesseg: Although many people think it is a mini Dobermann, it is in fact the older breed: it existed in Germany even before the Dobermann was bred.
orias-schnauzer.tagline: A bearded bodyguard in XXL: clever, strong, tireless.
orias-schnauzer.leiras: The Giant Schnauzer developed in Bavaria, in southern Germany, as a cattle-driving and farmyard guard dog and later became known as a police and service dog. Clever, strong, extremely energetic and decidedly protective, it is loyal to its family and reserved with strangers. Quick to learn but capable of being dominant, so it needs an experienced, consistent owner and lots of shared work. Its wiry coat hardly sheds but needs regular trimming or clipping, and it is worth keeping its beard clean after meals too.
orias-schnauzer.mozgas: 2 hours of exercise daily, with lots of working together
orias-schnauzer.erdekesseg: The name schnauzer comes from the German word “Schnauze” (muzzle, snout) and refers to the breed’s distinctive, bearded muzzle.
hovawart.tagline: The “guardian of the farmstead”: loyal, self-assured, family-centred.
hovawart.leiras: The Hovawart was re-bred in the 1920s from old-type farm dogs, modelled on the medieval German farmyard guard dogs. Self-assured, loyal and family-centred: at home it is a sweet, playful companion, yet it guards the house and its family firmly. A slow-maturing breed with a mind of its own, so it needs patient, consistent training and early socialisation. Because of its strong guarding instinct it is recommended more for experienced owners and is happiest in a house with a garden.
hovawart.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours of walking, running and working together daily
hovawart.erdekesseg: Its name comes from the Middle High German “hova” (yard, farm) and “wart” (guard), so it literally means “farmyard guardian”.
leonbergi.tagline: A lion-maned gentle giant – the children’s favourite cushion.
leonbergi.leiras: The Leonberger was born in the 19th century in the German town of Leonberg, traditionally bred using the Newfoundland, the Saint Bernard and the Pyrenean Mountain Dog. A calm, friendly and patient giant, especially gentle with children and always wanting to be close to its family. Quick to learn and happy to swim, but because of its size, good lead manners and basic obedience matter from puppyhood. Be prepared for very heavy shedding, drooling, high running costs and a shorter life expectancy of 8–10 years.
leonbergi.mozgas: A 1–1.5-hour gentle walk daily, going easy during puppyhood
leonbergi.erdekesseg: According to tradition, its breeder, Heinrich Essig, wanted a dog that resembled the lion on the coat of arms of the town of Leonberg.
pireneusi-hegyi-kutya.tagline: A white mountain giant who is on duty at night too – loudly.
pireneusi-hegyi-kutya.leiras: For centuries the Pyrenean Mountain Dog protected the flocks of Pyrenean shepherds from wolves and bears, and later became fashionable at the French royal court too. It is calm, gentle and patient with its family, but a decisive guardian towards strangers and unfamiliar animals. Bred to make independent decisions, it is not known for blind obedience and finds recall hard to learn. Be prepared for a lot of barking, mainly at night, and for its thick white coat to shed heavily.
pireneusi-hegyi-kutya.mozgas: 1 hour of gentle walking daily, plus free movement around the property
pireneusi-hegyi-kutya.erdekesseg: It has double dewclaws (two extra toes) on its hind legs, which the breed standard specifically requires.
bordeaux-i-dog.tagline: A wrinkle-browed French nobleman with an enormous head and heart.
bordeaux-i-dog.leiras: The Dogue de Bordeaux is one of the oldest French breeds, which for centuries guarded estates and assisted on big-game hunts. Calm, affectionate and very attached to its family, it is reserved with strangers, and because of its stubbornness it needs early socialisation and consistent training. It is important to know that its life expectancy is just 6–8 years, and because of its short muzzle it tolerates heat and exertion badly and gets out of breath easily. In some countries keeping the breed requires a permit, so look into the local rules.
bordeaux-i-dog.mozgas: 2–3 gentle walks daily, in hot weather only when it is cool
bordeaux-i-dog.erdekesseg: In the film “Turner & Hooch” (1989), Tom Hanks’s drooling four-legged partner, Hooch, was a Dogue de Bordeaux.
napolyi-masztiff.tagline: An ancient guardian wrapped in wrinkles – slow, dignified and drooling.
napolyi-masztiff.leiras: The Neapolitan Mastiff descends from the molossers of ancient Rome and for centuries guarded estates and farms in southern Italy. It is calm, dignified and deeply attached to its family, but suspicious of strangers, and it defends its home firmly. Because of its enormous strength and independence, it suits only a very experienced, consistent owner, and in some countries keeping one requires a permit. Expect heavy drooling, regular cleaning of the skin folds, and a dog that copes poorly with heat.
napolyi-masztiff.erdekesseg: In the Harry Potter films, Hagrid’s dog Fang was played by Neapolitan Mastiffs.
bullmasztiff.tagline: A silent gamekeeper’s dog: it doesn’t bark, it’s just there – and that’s enough.
bullmasztiff.leiras: The Bullmastiff was bred in 19th-century England by crossing the Mastiff with the Bulldog, to quietly pin down poachers alongside gamekeepers. Calm, well balanced and very affectionate, it is usually patient with children and almost never barks needlessly. Reserved with strangers, it is a confident guard dog, so it needs early socialisation and consistent training; in some countries keeping one requires a permit. Because of its great strength, walking on the lead must be taught from puppyhood, and expect some drooling too.
bullmasztiff.mozgas: 1 hour of gentle walking a day, going easy in hot weather
bullmasztiff.erdekesseg: In England it was once known as “the gamekeeper’s night dog”, because at night it patrolled the woods with the gamekeeper, on the trail of poachers.
shar-pei.tagline: A wrinkly little philosopher with a blue tongue and an independent spirit.
shar-pei.leiras: In southern China it spent centuries guarding peasant farms and helping with hunting, and for a time it was also used for fighting. A calm, clean and dignified dog, it is loyally attached to its family, but reserved with strangers, and it takes its watchdog duties seriously. It barks little and is fine in a flat, but it is strong-willed, so it needs early socialisation and patient, consistent training. Because of its distinctive wrinkles and narrow ear canals, its skin, eyes and ears need regular attention.
shar-pei.mozgas: About 1 hour of calm walking and play a day
shar-pei.erdekesseg: By the 1970s it had become so rare that in 1978 the Guinness Book of Records listed it as the rarest dog breed in the world.
kaukazusi-juhaszkutya.tagline: A mountain guardian with a bear’s courage – definitely not the hospitable type.
kaukazusi-juhaszkutya.leiras: For centuries, in the Caucasus mountains and on the steppes of southern Russia, it protected flocks and farmsteads from wolves and bears. Extremely brave, independent and territorial: it is loyal to its family, but greets strangers with suspicion and gives warning with a deep, loud bark, especially at night. It is not an obedience dog but a guardian that makes its own decisions, so it needs a very experienced, confident owner, thorough socialisation and a spacious, well-fenced property. In some countries keeping one requires a permit or is restricted, so check your local rules.
kaukazusi-juhaszkutya.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, plus a large fenced area
kaukazusi-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: Within the FCI (Fédération Cynologique Internationale), Russia is the breed’s country of patronage, because its planned breeding and uniform standard took shape in the Soviet Union from the 1920s onwards.
kozep-azsiai-juhaszkutya.tagline: The steppes’ ancient guardian: calm, independent, unshakeable.
kozep-azsiai-juhaszkutya.leiras: For centuries the pastoral peoples of Central Asia kept it to guard flocks, caravans and settlements, and its character was shaped by harsh steppe life. Calm, well balanced and confident, it defends its family and territory unshakeably, but is reserved with strangers. Very independent, it is not strong on unconditional obedience, so it suits only an experienced, level-headed and consistent owner, with early socialisation and a spacious, securely fenced property. In some countries keeping one requires a permit or is restricted, so check your local rules.
kozep-azsiai-juhaszkutya.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, plus a large fenced garden
kozep-azsiai-juhaszkutya.erdekesseg: In Turkmenistan, where it is known as the Alabai, it is a national symbol: in 2020 a giant gilded statue of it was erected in the capital, Ashgabat, and it even has its own holiday.
airedale-terrier.tagline: The king of terriers: big, brave and always up for a joke.
airedale-terrier.leiras: It developed in the mid-19th century in the valley of the River Aire in northern England, where it was used to hunt otters and rats, and later proved itself as a police and military dog too. Of the classic terriers it is the largest: clever, brave and playful, often a real clown, attached to its family, and an alert watchdog. It needs plenty of exercise and mental tasks and, true to a terrier, it has ideas of its own, so it needs patient, consistent training. It sheds little, but its wiry coat has to be trimmed several times a year.
airedale-terrier.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with running, play and tasks
airedale-terrier.erdekesseg: In the First World War the British Army used it as both a messenger and a guard dog, and it carried messages between the trenches.
welsh-terrier.tagline: Looks like a mini Airedale, but has a mind of its own: a cheerful Welsh rascal.
welsh-terrier.leiras: One of Britain’s oldest terrier breeds, used on the hill farms of Wales to hunt fox, badger and otter. Cheerful, friendly and more even-tempered than many of its terrier relatives, but curious, energetic and happy to bark. It does well in a flat if it gets enough exercise and shared play, and it usually gets on well with children. It sheds little, but its wiry coat needs regular trimming, and because of its strong hunting instinct, take care around small pets and when it is off the lead.
welsh-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking and active play a day
welsh-terrier.erdekesseg: President John F. Kennedy’s family dog, Charlie, was a Welsh Terrier, and Charlie and Pushinka – a gift from Khrushchev and a puppy of the Soviet space dog Strelka – even had a litter together.
kerry-blue-terrier.tagline: A blue-grey Irish rogue in velvety curls – though black as a puppy.
kerry-blue-terrier.leiras: In County Kerry in south-west Ireland it was the farmer’s all-rounder: it caught rats and otters, herded livestock and guarded the house. A lively, clever and affectionate dog, it is playful with its family, wary of strangers, and an excellent watchdog. It can be pushy with other dogs, so it needs early socialisation and a consistent, experienced hand. Its soft, wavy, blue-grey coat hardly sheds, but needs frequent brushing and clipping every few weeks.
kerry-blue-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking, play and a mental challenge a day
kerry-blue-terrier.erdekesseg: Michael Collins, the legendary figure of Ireland’s fight for independence, also kept a Kerry Blue Terrier and wanted to make the breed Ireland’s national dog.
border-terrier.tagline: An otter-headed, modest little terrier – the most laid-back of the daredevils.
border-terrier.leiras: Bred for fox hunting in the English–Scottish Border region: small enough to squeeze into a burrow, and long-legged enough to keep up with the hunters. Balanced, friendly and hardy, it is one of the easiest terriers to handle and gets on well with children too. Keen to learn and fine in a flat if it gets enough exercise, but because of its strong hunting instinct, stay alert around small pets and when it is off the lead. It loves to dig and explore, so the garden must be well fenced.
border-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walks, hiking and scent games a day
border-terrier.erdekesseg: The breed standard still requires it to be able to “follow a horse”, that is, to keep up with hunters on horseback.
skot-terrier.tagline: A dignified little Scottish gentleman, with a moustache and opinions of his own.
skot-terrier.leiras: Bred in the Scottish Highlands to hunt foxes, badgers and rodents, it was formerly also known as the Aberdeen Terrier. A dignified, brave and independent little dog, it is loyally attached to its family, reserved with strangers, and an alert watchdog. It is stubborn and does not tolerate rough handling, so it needs patient, consistent, reward-based training. Its wiry coat needs regular trimming, and it tolerates the bustle of small children less well than many other family dogs.
skot-terrier.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, with sniffing and play
skot-terrier.erdekesseg: US President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s inseparable companion, Fala, was a Scottish Terrier – his statue still stands next to his owner at the Roosevelt Memorial in Washington.
cairn-terrier.tagline: Toto’s breed from The Wizard of Oz: a shaggy, curious, brave little adventurer.
cairn-terrier.leiras: In the Scottish Highlands and on the Isle of Skye it was kept to hunt foxes and rodents lurking among piles of stones (cairns), which is where its name comes from. A cheerful, curious, brave and friendly little dog, a real tough adventurer that gets on well with children too. Even a first-time owner can cope with it, and it does fine in a flat, but it likes to bark and, given the chance, digs enthusiastically. Its shaggy, wiry coat sheds little; occasional brushing and a few trimmings a year are enough.
cairn-terrier.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking, play and sniffing a day
cairn-terrier.erdekesseg: Toto in The Wizard of Oz (1939) was played by a female Cairn Terrier called Terry, who appeared in many other films too.
bullterrier.tagline: A gladiator with an egg-shaped head and a clown’s soul – loves to play.
bullterrier.leiras: It developed in 19th-century England from Bulldog and terrier ancestors, and the breeder James Hinks made its distinctive egg-shaped head the breed’s trademark. Playful, funny and extremely affectionate, it wants to be near its owner almost all the time, but is rarely heard barking. Strong, energetic and stubborn, it needs consistent, patient training, plenty of shared exercise and early socialisation, especially around other dogs and small pets. In some countries keeping one requires a permit or is restricted, so check your local rules.
bullterrier.erdekesseg: US General George S. Patton’s faithful companion in the Second World War was a Bull Terrier called Willie.
drotszoru-foxterrier.tagline: The breed of Tintin’s Snowy: lively, daring, tireless.
drotszoru-foxterrier.leiras: Bred in England for fox hunting: its job was to bolt a fox that had gone to ground, out in front of the pack. Lively, daring, curious and playful, with loads of energy and humour, but wilful and happy to bark. It needs plenty of exercise, play and consistent training, otherwise it works off its tension by digging, chewing or yapping. It sheds little, but its wiry coat needs regular trimming, and because of its hunting instinct, take care around small pets.
drotszoru-foxterrier.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours of active exercise a day, with plenty of play and tasks
drotszoru-foxterrier.erdekesseg: At the Westminster Dog Show in New York it has won Best in Show more often than any other breed.
parson-russell-terrier.tagline: The Jack Russell Terrier’s longer-legged, even sportier cousin.
parson-russell-terrier.leiras: It descends from the fox-hunting terriers of John Russell, a Devon clergyman of the 19th century, and is now regarded as a breed separate from the shorter-legged Jack Russell Terrier: it got its longer legs for keeping up with hunters on horseback. A clever, brave, tenacious and astonishingly energetic little athlete that loves to work and play. If it doesn’t get enough exercise and tasks, it entertains itself by digging, barking and chewing. Its coat needs little grooming, but because of its strong hunting instinct, take care around small pets and when it is off the lead.
parson-russell-terrier.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours of active exercise a day, with running and tasks
parson-russell-terrier.erdekesseg: The breed’s foundation bitch was a white-and-tan female called Trump, whom the Reverend Russell bought from a milkman while still an Oxford student.
bedlington-terrier.tagline: A lion disguised as a lamb – soft curls, fast legs.
bedlington-terrier.leiras: In the 19th century it was kept for catching rats and rabbits in the mining district of Northumberland in northern England, around Bedlington. A real terrier lives behind its lamb-like looks: at home it is gentle, affectionate and calm, but outdoors it is a fast, tenacious and keen hunter. It does well in a flat and is usually kind with children, provided it gets its daily exercise. Its soft, curly coat sheds little, but needs regular brushing and clipping every few weeks.
bedlington-terrier.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day and, if possible, a free gallop in a fenced area
bedlington-terrier.erdekesseg: Puppies are born with dark coats, black or brown, and only lighten as they grow up to the characteristic pale bluish or sandy shade.
ir-buzaszinu-terrier.tagline: A wheaten ball of silk with Irish cheer – and a legendary greeting.
ir-buzaszinu-terrier.leiras: In Ireland it was long the all-rounder on small farms: it caught rats, herded livestock and guarded the yard. Cheerful, friendly and very people-oriented, it adores children and is famous for greeting arrivals with enthusiastic jumping, which is worth tackling from puppyhood. It is less suited to being a watchdog, because it makes friends with almost everyone, and training needs patience, since, true to a terrier, it can be wilful. Its silky coat sheds little but tangles easily, so it needs brushing almost daily.
ir-buzaszinu-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking, play and running a day
ir-buzaszinu-terrier.erdekesseg: Although it had long worked on Irish farms, the Irish Kennel Club only officially recognised it as a breed in its own right in 1937.
ir-terrier.tagline: A red daredevil – the Irish say it’s courage in canine form.
ir-terrier.leiras: One of the oldest Irish breeds: on farms it worked as a ratter, hunting dog and watchdog, and in the First World War it also proved itself as a messenger. Brave, daring and loyal, it is kind and playful with its family and children, wary of strangers, and an alert guard. It is prone to picking fights with other dogs, so it needs early socialisation and consistent training. Its red, wiry coat sheds little; weekly brushing and a few trimmings a year are enough.
ir-terrier.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking, running and play a day
ir-terrier.erdekesseg: The canine heroes of two Jack London novels, Jerry of the Islands and Michael, Brother of Jerry, are Irish Terriers too.
nemet-vadaszterrier.tagline: A professional hunter’s nature in a small body – not born for the sofa.
nemet-vadaszterrier.leiras: Created by German hunters after the First World War with nothing but hunting performance in mind, it is still used today for going to ground after quarry, driving wild boar and water work. Extremely brave, tenacious and a passionate hunter, it is loyal to its owner, suspicious of strangers, and raises a loud alarm. A tough, energetic working dog that needs serious work every day, with a hunting instinct that overrides almost everything. It is not recommended as a family pet or alongside small children or small pets, and is only truly happy with a hunter as its owner.
nemet-vadaszterrier.mozgas: 2 hours or more a day, preferably with hunting work
nemet-vadaszterrier.erdekesseg: The foundation of the breed was four black-and-tan terriers that zoo director Lutz Heck gave to one of the founders, Walter Zangenberg.
alaszkai-malamut.tagline: A powerful sled dog that would rather “talk” than bark – and loves snow.
alaszkai-malamut.leiras: The Alaskan Malamute is named after the Mahlemut Inuit of north-western Alaska, who kept them to haul heavy sleds and for hunting. Built not for speed but for strength and endurance, it is a friendly, cheerful, people-loving dog that greets everyone with enthusiasm, so it is unsuitable as a guard dog. It rarely barks, preferring to “talk” and howl, and when bored it likes to dig and destroy. Its independent, stubborn nature and strong hunting instinct call for consistent training, and its coat sheds heavily twice a year.
alaszkai-malamut.mozgas: 2 hours or more a day, with pulling and hiking, in cool weather
alaszkai-malamut.erdekesseg: Since 2010 the Alaskan Malamute has been Alaska’s official state dog.
keeshond.tagline: A bespectacled, smiling ball of fluff – a born family dog.
keeshond.leiras: The Keeshond (Wolfspitz) – Keeshond being its Dutch name – is the largest variety of German spitz, and was once the vigilant guardian of river barges and quays in Holland. A friendly, cheerful and decidedly people-oriented dog: patient with children, and following its family everywhere. It is excellent at sounding the alarm and announces every newcomer loudly, but it is not cut out to be a guard that bites. Its thick double coat needs brushing several times a week, it sheds heavily when it moults, and it does not cope well with being left alone for long.
keeshond.mozgas: 1 hour of walking and play a day
keeshond.erdekesseg: According to tradition, it got its Dutch name from the dog of the 18th-century Patriot leader Cornelis “Kees” de Gyselaer, so for a time the breed became a symbol of the Dutch Patriots.
japan-spicc.tagline: A snow-white mini Samoyed lookalike – cheerful, clean, adaptable.
japan-spicc.leiras: The Japanese Spitz developed in Japan in the first half of the 20th century, expressly as a companion dog. Cheerful, clever and affectionate, it enjoys playing with children and would go everywhere with its family. It adapts well to city flat life, learns easily and is good at dog sports too, but it announces strangers by barking. Its snow-white coat is surprisingly easy to keep clean, though it sheds heavily when it moults, so weekly brushing is a must.
japan-spicc.mozgas: 45–60 minutes of walking and play a day
amerikai-cocker-spaniel.mozgas: 45–60 minutes of walking and play a day
