japan-spicc.erdekesseg: Its ancestors were white German Spitzes taken to Japan in the early 20th century, so it is a close relative of the European spitzes.
eurazsiai.tagline: A well-balanced family spitz: reserved with strangers, devoted at home.
eurazsiai.leiras: The Eurasier is a young breed: it was developed in Germany in the 1960s by crossing the Keeshond (Wolfspitz) and the Chow Chow, later adding the Samoyed, expressly as a family dog. Calm, well balanced and quiet, it bonds deeply with its family and is reserved with strangers, but not aggressive. A sensitive soul, it copes badly with rough handling and with being kept in a kennel, and is happiest near its owners. Its thick coat needs regular brushing, and it sheds heavily when it moults.
eurazsiai.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of calm walking a day
eurazsiai.erdekesseg: A trait inherited from the Chow Chow, its tongue may be pink, bluish-black or spotted – the breed standard accepts all three.
basenji.tagline: The “barkless dog”: it yodels, and washes itself like a cat.
basenji.leiras: The Basenji is an ancient hunting dog of Central Africa, mainly the Congo Basin, where it drove game into nets. It does not bark but makes a characteristic, yodel-like sound, and grooms itself carefully like a cat, barely shedding. Clever, curious and independent, it only takes training seriously when it thinks it worthwhile, and because of its strong hunting instinct it easily runs off without a lead. When bored it entertains itself by chewing and destroying things, so it needs plenty of shared activities and play.
basenji.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day, with running in a fenced area
basenji.erdekesseg: Basenji bitches, like wolves, come into season only once a year, instead of the twice that is usual for most dog breeds.
csau-csau.tagline: A lion-maned, blue-tongued aristocrat with a cat’s independence.
csau-csau.leiras: The Chow Chow is one of China’s most ancient dog breeds, used for centuries for guarding, hunting and draught work. Dignified, independent and reserved: it bonds truly with just one or two people, eyes strangers with suspicion and does not like intrusive hugging. At home it is calm and notably clean, so it does fine in a flat, but it tolerates summer heat badly. Its thick coat needs regular, thorough brushing, and without early socialisation it can become overly suspicious.
csau-csau.mozgas: 45–60 minutes of calm walking a day, in summer during the cooler hours
csau-csau.erdekesseg: Sigmund Freud’s favourite dog, Jofi, was a Chow Chow, and often lay in the consulting room during therapy sessions.
amerikai-akita.tagline: A bear-headed, powerful guardian – the Akita’s bigger, sturdier branch.
amerikai-akita.leiras: The American Akita came to the United States after the Second World War, developed from larger, heavier-built Japanese Akitas, and is now regarded as a separate breed. A confident, dignified and quiet dog, it is deeply loyal to its family and firmly protects its territory and its people. It is reserved with strangers and often cannot get along with other dogs – especially those of the same sex. Its strong will calls for early, thorough socialisation and an experienced, consistent owner.
amerikai-akita.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking a day, mostly on the lead
amerikai-akita.erdekesseg: Helen Keller brought the first Akita to the United States in 1937, after being given it as a gift during her trip to Japan.
bloodhound.tagline: The world’s best nose, packed into droopy wrinkles.
bloodhound.leiras: The Bloodhound’s ancestor was the scenthound of the monks of the Saint-Hubert Abbey in the Ardennes in the Middle Ages, which is where the name St Hubert Hound comes from. A gentle, patient and friendly giant, kind with children, but not at all suited to guard duty. Once it catches a scent it forgets everything else, so it must never be let off the lead, and training takes a lot of patience. Its deep, booming voice carries a long way, it drools heavily, and its drooping ears need cleaning regularly.
bloodhound.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours of walking a day, with plenty of sniffing, on the lead
bloodhound.erdekesseg: In the United States, the scent-tracking results of Bloodhounds have even been accepted in court as evidence.
bajor-hegyi-vereb.tagline: The most persistent tracker of wounded game: the hunter’s secret weapon.
bajor-hegyi-vereb.leiras: The Bavarian Mountain Scent Hound was bred in Bavaria in the late 19th century to follow the blood trail of wounded game on mountain hunts. At home it is a calm, reserved dog, strongly attached to its owner and wary of strangers. At work it is extremely persistent and single-minded, a true specialist that needs regular tasks involving nose work. Without a job, cooped up in a small space, it gets bored, so it is recommended mainly for hunters or for owners who take tracking seriously.
bajor-hegyi-vereb.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with regular scent work
bajor-hegyi-vereb.erdekesseg: Its German name, Bayerischer Gebirgsschweißhund, comes from hunting jargon: here “Schweiß” means not sweat but the blood of wounded game.
angol-szetter.tagline: A speckled gentleman in a silky coat, with an endlessly sweet nature.
angol-szetter.leiras: The English Setter took its present form in 19th-century England as a bird-hunting gundog that signals found game by freezing motionless. Gentle, friendly and exceptionally sweet-natured, it is patient with children and open even to strangers, so it is no guard dog. Calm at home but tireless outdoors, it matures slowly and stays scatty and puppy-like for a long time. A sensitive soul, it takes harsh words badly, and its silky coat needs combing several times a week.
angol-szetter.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with plenty of free running
bretagne-i-spaniel.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with plenty of free running
angol-szetter.erdekesseg: Its distinctive fine speckled pattern is called “belton” – a word coined by Edward Laverack, one of the breed’s founders, from the name of a village in Northumberland.
angol-pointer.tagline: A living statue of the pointing hunter: stamina and elegance.
angol-pointer.leiras: The English Pointer developed in 17th–18th-century England and gets its name from the classic motionless stance, the “point”, with which it indicates game. A sporty, tireless and good-natured dog, affectionate with its family, patient with children and not suspicious even of strangers. It is only calm at home if it has had a proper run every day; otherwise it gets bored and restless. Its short coat needs hardly any grooming, but it tolerates cold badly, and because of its strong hunting instinct, recall needs to be practised separately.
angol-pointer.mozgas: 2 hours a day or more, with plenty of free running
angol-pointer.erdekesseg: In the Second World War, Judy, an English Pointer and the mascot of the Royal Navy, ended up in Japanese captivity, where she was even officially registered as a prisoner of war – she was later awarded the Dickin Medal.
drotszoru-nemet-vizsla.tagline: Any weather, any terrain: the hunter’s bearded all-rounder.
drotszoru-nemet-vizsla.leiras: The German Wirehaired Pointer was created in Germany at the turn of the 19th–20th century as a versatile hunting dog: it points game, retrieves, follows a trail and also works in water. Its hard, wiry coat and beard protect it in all weathers, so it is at home in thick undergrowth and in the cold. A clever, persistent dog, strongly attached to its family, it is more cautious with strangers than its short-haired relative and watchfully guards its home. Without several hours of active work or sport a day it gets bored, so it is not really recommended for beginners or city flats.
drotszoru-nemet-vizsla.mozgas: 2 hours a day or more, with running and retrieving
drotszoru-nemet-vizsla.erdekesseg: In the 1930s it also played a part in creating the Hungarian Wirehaired Vizsla: the Hungarian Vizsla was crossed with the German Wirehaired Pointer.
bretagne-i-spaniel.tagline: A compact French pointer with a spring in its step and a cheerful spirit.
bretagne-i-spaniel.leiras: The Brittany comes from the Brittany region of France, and although “spaniel” appears in its original name (Épagneul Breton), it actually works as a pointer: it finds game and signals it by standing on point. A compact, nimble and extremely enthusiastic dog, it is strongly attached to its family, plays cheerfully with children and gets on well with other dogs too. Quick to learn and keen to please, but sensitive, so it does not take a harsh tone well. Its energy is practically inexhaustible: without a good daily run and a job to do it becomes restless, so it suits an active, outdoor lifestyle.
bretagne-i-spaniel.erdekesseg: Many Brittanys are born with a naturally short tail, or with no tail at all.
flat-coated-retriever.tagline: A glossy black Peter Pan: never quite grows up.
flat-coated-retriever.leiras: The Flat-Coated Retriever developed in 19th-century England as a retrieving dog for water and land, and takes its name from its glossy, flat black or liver coat. Cheerful, friendly and eternally optimistic, it loves children and other dogs, and keeps its puppyish good humour into old age. Quick to learn but scatty for a long time, it needs plenty of exercise and shared activities. Sadly, cancers are common in the breed, so its lifespan is shorter than average.
flat-coated-retriever.mozgas: 2 hours a day, with running, swimming and retrieving
flat-coated-retriever.erdekesseg: In the late 19th and early 20th century it was one of the most popular retrievers among British gamekeepers, before the Labrador Retriever and the Golden Retriever pushed it into the background.
nova-scotia-retriever.tagline: Fox-coloured decoy dog: lures ducks in by playing.
nova-scotia-retriever.leiras: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever comes from the coast of Nova Scotia in Canada, where it played along the shore, fox-like, to lure curious wild ducks within shooting range, and then retrieved the shot game. The smallest of the retrievers, it is lively, clever and playful, devoted to its family and a little reserved with strangers at first. When excited it lets out a distinctive, sharp, shrieking sound that may surprise the neighbours. It needs a huge amount of exercise and mental challenge, and becomes restless when bored.
nova-scotia-retriever.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with running, swimming and retrieving
nova-scotia-retriever.erdekesseg: Since 1995 it has been the official provincial dog of Nova Scotia, Canada.
portugal-vizikutya.tagline: Curly-coated fisherman’s helper, born to swim – and it hardly sheds.
portugal-vizikutya.leiras: For centuries the Portuguese Water Dog helped the fishermen of the Algarve: it herded fish into the nets, swam out to fetch lost gear, and carried messages between boats. An excellent swimmer, clever, quick to learn and extremely energetic, it is strongly attached to its family and wants to be involved in everything. It sheds little, but its curly coat grows continuously, so it needs regular combing and clipping every few weeks. Without plenty of daily exercise and mental work it gets bored, and shows it by chewing and destroying things.
portugal-vizikutya.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, preferably with swimming
portugal-vizikutya.erdekesseg: The Obama family’s two dogs, Bo and Sunny, were both Portuguese Water Dogs, and lived in the White House for years.
spanyol-vizikutya.tagline: Curly-haired Spanish all-rounder: it herds, swims and learns.
spanyol-vizikutya.leiras: The Spanish Water Dog is the versatile working dog of Andalusia: for centuries it herded sheep and goats, helped fishermen and retrieved game from the water. Clever, hard-working and very loyal, it is closely attached to its family but initially reserved with strangers, so it needs early socialisation. Its curly coat sheds little and, instead of being combed, it is clipped evenly a few times a year. Without plenty of exercise and mental work it soon gets bored and finds its own entertainment, which is not always welcome.
spanyol-vizikutya.mozgas: 1.5–2 hours a day, with plenty of shared work and swimming
spanyol-vizikutya.erdekesseg: In its homeland of Andalusia it used to be called “turco andaluz”, meaning “Andalusian Turk”.
amerikai-cocker-spaniel.tagline: The English Cocker’s elegant American cousin, in a long, lush coat.
amerikai-cocker-spaniel.leiras: The American Cocker Spaniel developed from the English Cocker Spaniel in the United States and became a separate breed in the mid-20th century: smaller, rounder-headed and with a much fuller coat than its European relative. A sweet, cheerful and affectionate companion, it enjoys learning, gets on well with children and is content in a flat as long as it gets enough attention. A sensitive soul, it takes harsh words badly. Its long, silky coat, however, is a serious commitment: it needs regular combing, a groomer every 4–8 weeks and careful ear care.
amerikai-cocker-spaniel.erdekesseg: Lady, the heroine of Disney’s 1955 classic Lady and the Tramp, is an American Cocker Spaniel.
kooikerhondje.leiras: For centuries in the Netherlands the Kooikerhondje worked at duck decoys (trapping ponds): waving its white, plumed tail, it lured curious ducks in, and in the mid-20th century a Dutch baroness saved it from extinction. A cheerful, nimble and affectionate dog, cuddly and playful with its family, quick to learn and happy in a flat if it gets enough exercise. A sensitive nature: it is often reserved with strangers and copes badly with rough handling and noisy, chaotic surroundings. It therefore needs careful socialisation and patient, positive training.
kooikerhondje.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day of walks, play and dog sports
kooikerhondje.erdekesseg: Its name literally means “the little dog of the duck-trap man”: the Dutch “kooi” is the name of a channelled trap built for catching wild ducks.
lhasa-apso.tagline: Tiny sentry of Tibetan monasteries, in a lush, floor-length coat.
lhasa-apso.leiras: The Lhasa Apso was the indoor guard dog of Tibetan monasteries and noble houses, announcing newcomers with sharp barking. Today it is still a watchful, confident and independent little dog: deeply attached to its family, wary of strangers and quick to announce every unusual noise loudly. Its thick, floor-length coat sheds little, but needs daily combing or regular clipping, and its stubborn nature calls for patient, consistent training. Because of its shorter muzzle it copes less well with heat, and mild breathing problems can occur, so choose a puppy from health-screened parents.
lhasa-apso.erdekesseg: It is named after Tibet’s holy city, Lhasa, and its Tibetan name, “Abso Seng Kye”, means roughly “barking lion guard dog”.
tibeti-terrier.tagline: Not actually a terrier: a shaggy Tibetan good-luck charm.
tibeti-terrier.leiras: The Tibetan Terrier lived in Himalayan monasteries and alongside nomadic families, where it was regarded as a good-luck companion – despite its name, it is not actually a terrier. A cheerful, gentle and adaptable dog, closely attached to its family, patient with children and a little reserved with strangers at first. It is happy in a flat or a house with a garden as long as it can walk and play every day. Its thick, long coat sheds little, but it must be combed through thoroughly several times a week, or it quickly gets matted.
tibeti-terrier.mozgas: 45–60 minutes a day of walking and playing together
tibeti-terrier.erdekesseg: Its large, flat, round paws work like snowshoes, so it moves more easily over snowy, rocky mountain terrain.
pekingi-palotakutya.tagline: A lion-hearted imperial lapdog – and well aware of it.
pekingi-palotakutya.leiras: For centuries the Pekingese was the treasured favourite of the Chinese imperial court. A dignified, independent and brave little dog, it is loyally attached to its owner, but it is stubborn and dislikes the romping and rougher hands of small children. Its exercise needs are small and it is perfectly happy in a flat, but its thick coat sheds heavily and needs regular combing and cleaning of the facial folds. Its flat nose often causes breathing difficulties (brachycephalic syndrome) and it tolerates heat very badly, so choose a puppy only from health-screened parents.
pekingi-palotakutya.mozgas: 20–30 minutes a day of gentle walking; in hot weather, only in the cool
pekingi-palotakutya.erdekesseg: In 1860, after the sacking of the Summer Palace in Beijing, British soldiers took the first dogs to England, and one of them was given as a gift to Queen Victoria.
papillon.tagline: Butterfly-eared mini genius – the star of the agility course.
papillon.leiras: The Papillon, or “butterfly dog”, was a favourite at the courts of Renaissance Europe and often sits on noble ladies’ laps in old paintings. Despite its tiny size it is lively, curious and extremely clever: it learns quickly, loves tricks and is among the best on the agility course. Its silky coat has no undercoat and needs surprisingly little grooming, and it does very well in a flat. Because of its fragile bones, though, rough play from small children and big jumps can easily injure it.
papillon.mozgas: 45–60 minutes a day of walking and plenty of play together
papillon.erdekesseg: The drop-eared variety is called the Phalène, meaning “night moth” – the counterpart to the erect-eared “butterfly”.
coton-de-tulear.tagline: A cotton-wool grinner from Madagascar who charms everyone.
coton-de-tulear.leiras: The Coton de Tuléar is related to the bichons, and in Madagascar it was a favourite lapdog of the local nobility. Cheerful, gentle and extremely sociable, it gets on with children, strangers and other animals, barks little, and is an excellent choice even for a first-time owner. Its cotton-like white coat sheds little, but must be combed through thoroughly several times a week or it gets matted. It is very attached to its person, so it finds long periods alone hard to bear.
coton-de-tulear.erdekesseg: It is named after its cotton-like coat (French “coton”) and the Madagascan port city of Tuléar (now Toliara).
kinai-meztelen-kutya.tagline: Punk-haired fashion icon: no coat, but all the more love.
kinai-meztelen-kutya.leiras: The origins of the Chinese Crested are obscure, and today’s breed was developed mainly in England and America in the 20th century. It comes in two varieties: the hairless, which has silky hair only on its head, tail and feet, and the fully coated Powderpuff. A sweet, playful and very affectionate lapdog, it barks little and does very well in a flat. Its bare skin does need care, though: regular cleaning and moisturising, sunscreen in summer and a jumper in winter.
kinai-meztelen-kutya.mozgas: 30–45 minutes a day of walking, with sunscreen in sunshine
kinai-meztelen-kutya.erdekesseg: Hairlessness is caused by a dominant gene, so a single litter can contain both hairless puppies and puppies with a full coat, known as Powderpuffs.
brusszeli-griffon.tagline: Bearded, human-faced little character who takes everything seriously.
brusszeli-griffon.leiras: The Brussels Griffon once caught rats in the cab stables of the Belgian capital, and then, in the late 19th century, became a fashionable lapdog as the favourite of Queen Marie Henriette of Belgium. A confident, very affectionate little dog with an almost human expression, it often bonds most closely with one person and reacts sensitively to rough handling. Its wiry coat sheds little but needs trimming a few times a year. Its flat nose can cause breathing difficulties (brachycephalic syndrome) and it tolerates heat poorly, so choose a puppy only from health-screened parents.
brusszeli-griffon.mozgas: 30–45 minutes a day of walking and play, less in hot weather
brusszeli-griffon.erdekesseg: In the 1997 film “As Good as It Gets”, starring Jack Nicholson, Verdell, the neighbour’s dog, was played by Brussels Griffons.
angol-agar.tagline: The dog world’s racing car, happiest parked on the sofa.
angol-agar.leiras: The Greyhound is an ancient British hunting dog, known today mainly as a racing sighthound – in Europe many retired racing dogs find new families through rescue organisations. At home it is surprisingly calm, gentle and quiet: after short, lightning-fast sprints it spends most of the day dozing on the sofa, and it rarely barks. Its short coat needs almost no grooming, but because of its thin skin and low body fat it feels the cold, so it needs a coat in winter. With its strong prey drive it may chase cats and small animals, so only let it run off the lead in a fenced area.
angol-agar.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, including short, safe sprints
angol-agar.erdekesseg: It is the fastest dog breed: in a sprint it can reach speeds of around 70 km/h.
ir-farkaskutya.tagline: One of the tallest dogs, with the gentlest heart.
ir-farkaskutya.leiras: The Irish Wolfhound is an ancient Irish hunting dog that once hunted wolves and deer; after it had almost died out by the 19th century, Captain George Augustus Graham revived it by breeding. Despite its huge size it is a gentle, calm and patient giant, kind with children, rarely barking and, for that very reason, no watchdog. It needs a lot of space, and its costs are giant too, from food to the vet. A short-lived breed, living 6–10 years on average, it needs careful, gradual exercise as a puppy.
ir-farkaskutya.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of calm walking a day, with some free running
ir-farkaskutya.erdekesseg: Since 1902 the mascot of the Irish Guards regiment of the British Army has always been an Irish Wolfhound.
barzoj.tagline: Aristocratic Russian sighthound with a long, silky coat.
barzoj.leiras: The Borzoi is the sighthound of the Russian aristocracy, kept in large packs for hunting wolves, foxes and hares. At home it is calm, dignified and quiet, gentle with its family and rather reserved with strangers, and it does not like loud, chaotic romping. Independent-minded, it needs patient training, and because of its strong prey drive it should only be let off the lead in a fenced area. Its long, silky coat needs thorough combing every week, and it sheds heavily when moulting.
barzoj.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours of walking a day, including safe off-lead running
barzoj.erdekesseg: Its Russian name, “borzaya”, comes from the word “borzyi”, meaning swift, fast.
afgan-agar.tagline: A shimmering, floor-length coat, royal bearing – and a will of its own.
afgan-agar.leiras: The Afghan Hound hunted hares and gazelle in the mountains of Afghanistan, and its thick coat protected it through the harsh, cold winters. Dignified, independent and wary of strangers, but affectionate with its family and sometimes downright clownish. Independent-minded, it needs a great deal of patience in training, and because of its strong prey drive it should only be let off the lead in a safe, fenced area. Its floor-length, silky coat is a real commitment: it needs several hours of combing a week and regular bathing.
afgan-agar.mozgas: 1–1.5 hours a day, including safe off-lead running
afgan-agar.erdekesseg: The world’s first cloned dog, Snuppy, born in South Korea in 2005, was an Afghan Hound.
saluki.tagline: The gazelle hunter of the ancient Middle East: graceful, quiet, independent.
saluki.leiras: The Saluki is one of the oldest dog breeds: in the deserts of the Middle East, the Bedouin hunted gazelle and hares with it. At home it is quiet, gentle and dignified, attached to its family but not clingy, and rather reserved with strangers. Outdoors, though, it is a tireless runner that regularly needs to race freely in a safe, fenced area. An independent and sensitive nature: training calls for patience and a gentle touch, and because of its strong prey drive its recall is seldom reliable.
saluki.erdekesseg: In the Middle East it was traditionally hunted together with a hunting falcon: the bird slowed the gazelle down and the Saluki caught up with it.
spanyol-galgo.tagline: Perhaps Europe’s most-rescued sighthound – a grateful, gentle, quiet housemate.
spanyol-galgo.leiras: For centuries the Galgo Español has been the hare-hunting sighthound of Spain’s fields, and today it is known across Europe: a great many galgos discarded from hunting find new homes through rescue organisations. At home it is a calm, gentle and quiet housemate that almost never barks and happily dozes through most of the day. Rescued dogs are often timid at first, so they need patient, gentle handling and gradual settling in. Its short coat needs hardly any grooming, but its strong prey drive means it may chase small animals, and it should only be let off the lead in a fenced area.
spanyol-galgo.mozgas: About 1 hour of walking a day, including safe off-lead running
spanyol-galgo.erdekesseg: The word “galgo” comes from the Latin “canis gallicus”, meaning “Gaulish dog”, which is what the Romans called the sighthounds of the Celts.
